01 · Exploratory Data Analysis & Feature Engineering¶

Pod Nova · 10Alytics × JengaGlobal Q3 Students Hackathon 2026 · Track C: Data Science

Purpose. Understand the AI-Powered Job Market Insights dataset before any modelling: check its quality, describe each field, test which factors are associated with Automation_Risk, and build the engineered features used by the model and the career-mapping system.

Deliverables served: EDA & Feature Engineering · Workforce Insights & Visualizations

Section Question it answers
1. Setup —
2. Data quality audit Is the data complete, consistent, and as described?
3. Univariate profile What does each field look like on its own?
4. Association with risk Which factors move with displacement risk?
5. Feature interdependence Are the fields related to each other the way real labour data would be?
6. Skill profiles by role Which roles share skills (foundation for career mapping)?
7. Engineered features Do exposure-based features add signal?
8. Key findings What this means for modelling and for the solution

Reading this. The file is complete (no missing values, no duplicates). Five salary values sit outside the 1.5 × IQR range; they are plausible for the roles and cities involved, so they are retained rather than removed.

The brief describes three fields as numeric (AI adoption as a 0–1 index, growth as a percentage, skills as a list). In the data they are ordered categories and a single skill per row. This is documented in docs/data_dictionary.md and shapes the encoding choices in Section 7.

Reading this. The three risk classes are near-equal (≈ ⅓ each), so accuracy and macro-F1 will tell the same story and no class rebalancing is needed. Chance-level performance for a 3-class model is therefore ≈ 0.33, which is the bar any model must clear. Every categorical field is also spread fairly evenly across its levels.

4. Association with automation risk¶

For each categorical feature we run a chi-square test of independence against Automation_Risk, measure effect size with Cramér's V (0 = no association, 0.1 ≈ small, 0.3 ≈ medium, 0.5 ≈ large), and correct the p-values for testing eight features at once using the Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate procedure. Salary is tested with a Kruskal–Wallis test (no normality assumption).

In [7]:
def cramers_v(x, y):
    table = pd.crosstab(x, y)
    chi2, p, dof, _ = chi2_contingency(table)
    n = table.values.sum(); r, k = table.shape
    return np.sqrt((chi2 / n) / (min(r, k) - 1)), chi2, dof, p

rows = []
for col in cat_features:
    v, chi2, dof, p = cramers_v(df[col], df[TARGET])
    r, k = df[col].nunique(), df[TARGET].nunique()
    v_chance = np.sqrt((dof / len(df)) / (min(r, k) - 1))  # E[chi2] = dof under independence
    rows.append({"feature": col, "chi2": chi2, "dof": dof, "p_value": p,
                 "cramers_v": v, "v_expected_by_chance": v_chance})
assoc = pd.DataFrame(rows)
assoc["p_adjusted_BH"] = multipletests(assoc["p_value"], method="fdr_bh")[1]
assoc["significant_after_correction"] = assoc["p_adjusted_BH"] < 0.05
assoc = assoc.sort_values("cramers_v", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)

groups = [g["Salary_USD"].values for _, g in df.groupby(TARGET)]
H, p_kw = kruskal(*groups)
print(f"Salary vs risk (Kruskal-Wallis): H = {H:.2f}, p = {p_kw:.3f}")
assoc.round(3)

Salary vs risk (Kruskal-Wallis): H = 6.32, p = 0.043

Reading this. After correcting for multiple testing, no feature is significantly associated with automation risk. The Cramér's V values look like small effects, but for fields with 10 levels and 500 rows, chance alone produces V of about 0.13, so the observed values sit essentially at the chance line. Job title comes closest (V = 0.17, unadjusted p = 0.04, adjusted p = 0.34), and its pattern does not follow any real-world logic: Cybersecurity Analysts show the most High-risk postings, Operations Managers the fewest. Salary shows a small nominal difference (Kruskal–Wallis p = 0.04, with Medium-risk roles paid slightly less than both Low and High), which does not survive correction for the number of tests run and has no sensible direction.

For a real labour-market dataset we would expect clear structure here (for example, roles built on routine code or reporting carrying more risk). Its absence is the most important finding of the EDA: the features in this dataset carry little or no information about the risk label. Section 5 checks whether the fields are related to each other at all.

5. Feature interdependence¶

In real job-market data, fields are connected: AI Researchers mostly need Machine Learning, Sales Managers mostly need Sales skills, and salaries cluster by role and city. This heatmap shows Cramér's V between every pair of categorical fields.

In [10]:
all_cat = cat_features + [TARGET]
V = pd.DataFrame(np.eye(len(all_cat)), index=all_cat, columns=all_cat)
for i, a in enumerate(all_cat):
    for b in all_cat[i+1:]:
        V.loc[a, b] = V.loc[b, a] = cramers_v(df[a], df[b])[0]
Vp = V.iloc[1:, :-1]
mask = np.triu(np.ones_like(Vp, dtype=bool), k=1)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 6.5))
sns.heatmap(Vp.values, mask=mask, cmap=sns.light_palette("#104281", as_cmap=True), vmin=0, vmax=0.5,
            annot=True, fmt=".2f", annot_kws={"size": 8.5}, linewidths=2, linecolor=SURFACE,
            xticklabels=[c.replace("_", " ") for c in Vp.columns],
            yticklabels=[c.replace("_", " ") for c in Vp.index], cbar_kws={"label": "Cramér's V", "shrink": 0.7}, ax=ax)
ax.set_title("Fields are nearly independent of one another")
plt.xticks(rotation=40, ha="right"); save(fig, "06_feature_independence"); plt.show()
off_diag = V.values[np.triu_indices(len(all_cat), 1)]
print(f"Largest pairwise Cramér's V: {off_diag.max():.2f} | median: {np.median(off_diag):.2f}")

Largest pairwise Cramér's V: 0.20 | median: 0.11

Reading this. Every pair of fields is only weakly related, at the V ≈ 0.10–0.15 level that chance produces at this sample size. Job titles are not tied to the skills you would expect, and nothing clusters by industry or location. This pattern is consistent with a dataset whose columns were generated largely independently. We state this openly: it sets a ceiling on what any model can learn from this data, and it is why our solution pairs the required ML model with a transparent, research-informed exposure index and a validity audit.

6. Skill profiles by role (foundation for career mapping)¶

Because each posting lists one skill, a role's skill profile is the share of its postings that require each skill. Roles with similar profiles are candidate transition pathways.

Reading this. The profiles do not match what these jobs look like in practice. Only 4% of AI Researcher postings require Machine Learning, only 6% of UX Designer postings require UX/UI Design, and Project Management is the most common UX Designer skill (26%). This is further evidence that the fields were generated independently.

For the career-mapping system this is workable: each role draws on a mix of skills, so profiles overlap and similarity between roles can be measured (cosine similarity on these rows is the basis of the career-mapping system). Growth share and median salary per role give the market-demand and pay signals that recommendations will weigh.

7. Engineered features¶

The model-ready features are built in src/features.py so the same logic is reused by the model and the app.

Feature Definition Why
ai_adoption_ord, company_size_ord, growth_ord Ordered categories encoded 0 / 1 / 2 Keeps their natural order, which one-hot encoding would discard
remote_flag 1 if remote-friendly Binary encoding
skill_exposure Task Exposure Index: research-informed 0–1 weight for how automatable a skill is Brings external knowledge about generative-AI exposure into the model
ai_pressure skill_exposure × adoption / 2 Exposure only bites where the employer is actually adopting AI
salary_pct_in_title Salary percentile within the same job title Separates pay level from role
vulnerability_signal ai_pressure × (1 − growth / 2) High exposure, high adoption, and shrinking demand together

One-hot encoding of nominal fields and scaling of numeric fields happen inside the model pipeline, so they learn only from training data (no leakage).

Reading this. The engineered features encode real-world knowledge about which work generative AI can do, but they are not associated with this dataset's risk label either. This is what we expect if the label was not generated from the job's characteristics. We keep them in the model (the permutation test in the modelling notebook will show formally whether they help) and, more importantly, in the app, where the exposure index gives users an interpretable, research-grounded view that does not depend on the label.

8. Key findings¶

1. The data is clean but does not match the brief. 500 complete records, no duplicates, 5 plausible salary outliers retained. Three fields described as numeric are ordered categories, each posting lists one skill, and the job titles at the centre of the scenario (Data Analyst, BI Developer) are absent.

2. The risk label is balanced: Low 32%, Medium 35%, High 34%. Chance-level performance for a 3-class model is therefore about 0.33 on accuracy and macro-F1.

3. No feature is associated with automation risk. After Benjamini–Hochberg correction, none of the eight categorical features is significant (all adjusted p ≥ 0.34), and every Cramér's V sits at roughly the level chance produces at this sample size. Salary shows only a small nominal difference with no sensible direction.

4. The fields are nearly independent of one another (median pairwise Cramér's V 0.11, maximum 0.20), and role–skill pairings contradict real-world job content (for example, 4% of AI Researcher postings require Machine Learning). The dataset behaves as if its columns were generated separately.

5. Research-informed engineered features do not change this. The Task Exposure Index, AI pressure, and vulnerability signal show no difference across risk classes (Kruskal–Wallis p = 0.33 to 0.67).

6. Market signals do vary by role and are usable. Growth share ranges from 23% (Marketing Specialist) to 43% (Operations Manager); decline share from 16% to 48%. Together with skill profiles and salary, these support the career-mapping system.

What this means for the solution¶

  • Modelling: we will build and tune the required multi-class classifier properly, but expect performance close to chance. A label permutation test will establish formally whether the model has learned anything real, and we will report the result honestly rather than over-state accuracy.
  • Decision support: because the label is not informative, the app will lead with the transparent Task Exposure Index and skill-adjacency recommendations, and present the ML prediction with its measured reliability.
  • Responsible use: predictions about people's livelihoods should never rest on a model that cannot beat chance. Showing this clearly, and building a framework that becomes predictive once connected to real HR and labour-market data (e.g. O*NET task statements), is the core contribution.
